item.text: {"chapter_id":"6B","answers":[{"question_id":"6B.1","answer":"López Obrador made welfare an explicit governing purpose through “Primero los pobres,” expanded pensions, transfers, minimum-wage increases, and a 2023 social-program budget increase; IMSS-BIENESTAR also formally committed to free, universal, rights-based care. These were funded and partly implemented: the older-adult pension expanded to 10.8 million recipients by 2022, and CONEVAL estimated transfers reduced 2022 poverty. However, universalization sometimes displaced targeted programs, the poorest group’s share of social spending reportedly fell, and health and other deprivations worsened. The evidence therefore supports a genuine welfare priority, but one mixed with political centralization, weak targeting, fiscal concerns, and incomplete delivery. Attribution is strong for presidential priorities and federal program design, weaker for aggregate outcomes because remittances, wages, subnational action, the pandemic, and external conditions also mattered. The 2023 evidence measures budgets and institutional commitments more reliably than end-period welfare effects.","supporting_evidence_ids":["BATCH-0038-E001","BATCH-0012-E002","BATCH-0049-E006","BATCH-0032-E006","BATCH-0051-E001","BATCH-0052-E001","BATCH-0052-E010","BATCH-0048-E014"],"contrary_or_qualifying_evidence_ids":["BATCH-0012-E016","BATCH-0031-E015","BATCH-0032-E002","BATCH-0032-E003","BATCH-0050-E002","BATCH-0038-E005","BATCH-0047-E004"],"limitations_and_gaps":["Most outcome evidence ends in 2022 rather than 2023.","The index lacks a complete 2023 incidence and expenditure-execution assessment across all welfare domains.","Presidential attribution is clearer for priorities and programs than for national outcomes."]},{"question_id":"6B.2","answer":"Access improvements were substantial in transfers, pensions, minimum wages, food security, and some labor and migrant services. The adult pension expanded in coverage and value; 2022 food insecurity, housing-quality deprivation, and basic-service deprivation were lower than in 2018; and transfer counterfactuals indicate some poverty reduction. Formal IMSS-BIENESTAR rules promised free services, medicines, itinerant care, complaint systems, and thousands of facilities. Implementation and effective uptake were much weaker in health and education: health-service deprivation rose sharply, public care fell while private and pharmacy care increased, catastrophic spending rose, medicine shortages were severe, education spending remained low and inequitable, and migrant shelters and asylum services were overloaded. Rules and budgets demonstrate conduct and intended implementation, but outcomes show mixed quality, affordability, continuity, and regional access. The health deterioration is plausibly linked to Seguro Popular’s abolition, INSABI, and later IMSS-BIENESTAR transition, though survey changes, the pandemic, and other factors qualify causation.","supporting_evidence_ids":["BATCH-0032-E004","BATCH-0032-E006","BATCH-0032-E009","BATCH-0051-E001","BATCH-0051-E002","BATCH-0051-E003","BATCH-0052-E010","BATCH-0052-E017","BATCH-0054-E002"],"contrary_or_qualifying_evidence_ids":["BATCH-0003-E005","BATCH-0032-E003","BATCH-0032-E010","BATCH-0031-E017","BATCH-0048-E001","BATCH-0048-E002","BATCH-0013-E006","BATCH-0015-E005","BATCH-0015-E017","BATCH-0050-E015"],"limitations_and_gaps":["There is no complete 2023 service-uptake or quality series for health, education, water, sanitation, housing, and food.","Formal IMSS-BIENESTAR entitlements are not proof of nationwide delivery.","Regional and group-level incidence is incomplete outside poverty and selected migrant evidence."]},{"question_id":"6B.3","answer":"The administration enacted and funded several group-oriented measures: universal older-adult pensions, disability transfers, scholarships, migrant-child protection rules, Indigenous consultation requirements, gender-violence laws, and programs directed toward poorer southern regions. Older adults experienced marked reductions in poverty and pension-related deprivation, while transfers reduced aggregate poverty. Yet targeting and incidence were uneven: disability and Indigenous populations retained very high poverty and multiple deprivations; children’s health deprivation and extreme poverty worsened; poor regions and rural households remained more deprived; migrant children were frequently underserved, detained, or exposed to inadequate shelter; and women continued to face gender violence, labor-market disadvantage, and inadequate services. Some programs lacked clear target populations, coverage indicators, or sufficient staffing. The evidence supports real priority-setting and some delivered protection, but not consistently equitable protection or effective enforcement. Attribution is strongest for federal program design and funding, weaker for subnational implementation and aggregate group outcomes.","supporting_evidence_ids":["BATCH-0032-E004","BATCH-0032-E005","BATCH-0032-E006","BATCH-0032-E007","BATCH-0032-E009","BATCH-0015-E004","BATCH-0051-E001","BATCH-0052-E003","BATCH-0054-E004"],"contrary_or_qualifying_evidence_ids":["BATCH-0032-E005","BATCH-0032-E007","BATCH-0053-E010","BATCH-0054-E003","BATCH-0051-E025","BATCH-0015-E003","BATCH-0015-E005","BATCH-0015-E007","BATCH-0044-E009","BATCH-0051-E009"],"limitations_and_gaps":["Incidence data are strongest for poverty, pensions, disability, Indigenous groups, children, and migrants, but incomplete for older people, women, and other marginalized groups.","Many group outcomes end in 2022 or reflect joint federal-state-donor action.","The index does not establish the personal presidential role in each subnational violation or reform."]},{"question_id":"6B.4","answer":"There were some professional and administrative mechanisms: IMSS-BIENESTAR rules required training, multidisciplinary supervision, performance review, procurement controls, audits, citizen oversight, and external evaluation; migrant-child programs created formal coordination and protection roles; and CONEVAL provided technical monitoring. However, broader evidence points to weakened state capacity through austerity, preference for loyal rather than technically qualified officials, underfunded and understaffed protection and service institutions, health-unit reductions, medicine-logistics problems, and serious migrant-child and shelter staffing gaps. Segalmex procurement and diversion investigations further show that food-service administration was vulnerable to irregular contracting and weak controls, even though corrective audits and investigations occurred. Thus formal professional standards existed, and some capacity expanded, but actual staffing, procurement transparency, retention, and implementation were inconsistent. Presidential attribution is strong for centralization, austerity, agency creation, and major appointments; operational failures often involved agencies and subnational authorities.","supporting_evidence_ids":["BATCH-0051-E004","BATCH-0051-E005","BATCH-0051-E006","BATCH-0015-E004","BATCH-0015-E005","BATCH-0032-E006","BATCH-0026-E006","BATCH-0048-E010"],"contrary_or_qualifying_evidence_ids":["BATCH-0007-E003","BATCH-0011-E001","BATCH-0046-E008","BATCH-0015-E007","BATCH-0018-E004","BATCH-0018-E014","BATCH-0013-E006","BATCH-0050-E005","BATCH-0050-E002"],"limitations_and_gaps":["The index does not provide a comprehensive personnel roster, qualification audit, or retention data.","Procurement evidence is concentrated in Segalmex and does not represent every social-service agency.","Some critical administrative assessments are interpretive or pre-2023."]},{"question_id":"6B.5","answer":"Mexico retained substantial measurement and evaluation capacity. CONEVAL published multidimensional poverty indicators, program databases, evaluations, monitoring products, and 173 evaluations in 2023; it reported high dissemination and completion of improvement commitments. IMSS-BIENESTAR rules required indicators, audits, complaints, social auditing, external evaluation, and public reporting, while poverty and planning instruments used disaggregated demographic and geographic data. Corrective capacity is visible in health-system reorganization, medicine-warehouse creation, and some program-design improvements. But the evidence does not show consistent presidential use of findings to correct failure. Several programs had unclear populations, weak or absent outcome indicators, poor logical links, no coverage indicators, or insufficient performance; health access deteriorated sharply; Segalmex irregularities persisted; and official data had reconciliation and subnational-coverage gaps. Independent reports also identified opacity, missing distribution reports, and resistance or weakness in oversight institutions. The conduct of measurement is therefore well evidenced, while timely correction, transparency, and accountability are mixed.","supporting_evidence_ids":["BATCH-0006-E003","BATCH-0013-E007","BATCH-0031-E019","BATCH-0051-E004","BATCH-0051-E005","BATCH-0051-E006","BATCH-0052-E002","BATCH-0052-E006","BATCH-0054-E007"],"contrary_or_qualifying_evidence_ids":["BATCH-0012-E016","BATCH-0007-E003","BATCH-0011-E001","BATCH-0018-E017","BATCH-0026-E014","BATCH-0052-E008","BATCH-0052-E015","BATCH-0032-E003","BATCH-0048-E009"],"limitations_and_gaps":["CONEVAL’s institutional performance is partly self-reported and does not prove executive compliance.","The index rarely documents a completed correction tied explicitly to a specific evaluation finding.","Some official data have comparability, coverage, or reporting limitations."]},{"question_id":"6B.6","answer":"Preparedness and crisis responses were mixed. Formal disaster-finance, risk-transfer, climate, health, social-protection, and IMSS-BIENESTAR mechanisms existed, and emergency exercises identified improvements in hospitals, shelters, information, and command systems. During Hurricane Otis, the government deployed troops, workers, air and naval bridges, and reconstruction structures; during migration and other emergencies, federal and UN partners expanded shelter, education, health, and protection support. These actions show operational mobilization and some preparedness. Conversely, Otis produced delayed or uneven assistance, shortages of water, food, medicine, fuel, and communications, and limited early information; vulnerable residents received little help in early reporting. The El Bosque displacement response left families without promised relocation and basic services, while earlier disaster responses showed weak plans, transparency, coordination, and follow-up. Migration and shelter capacity were overwhelmed, and fiscal reserves and health capacity were constrained. Attribution is strong for federal crisis choices and resource deployment but shared with states, municipalities, donors, and the novelty or scale of shocks.","supporting_evidence_ids":["BATCH-0002-E010","BATCH-0014-E016","BATCH-0051-E002","BATCH-0015-E011","BATCH-0015-E012","BATCH-0015-E015","BATCH-0050-E010","BATCH-0031-E003"],"contrary_or_qualifying_evidence_ids":["BATCH-0003-E022","BATCH-0029-E003","BATCH-0044-E009","BATCH-0018-E007","BATCH-0017-E003","BATCH-0053-E007","BATCH-0015-E017","BATCH-0040-E009"],"limitations_and_gaps":["Otis evidence is largely an early-response snapshot and does not establish final recovery outcomes.","The index does not provide a full pandemic, famine, displacement, or economic-shock counterfactual.","Preparedness exercise findings are self-reported and do not establish closure of identified weaknesses."]},{"question_id":"6B.7","answer":"Formal safeguards against political allocation existed in some programs: Jóvenes Construyendo el Futuro prohibited electoral proselytism; IMSS-BIENESTAR rules promised equal, free, confidential care, complaint systems, citizen oversight, and non-discrimination; and program rules defined eligibility and monitoring. Courts, CNDH, CONEVAL, and independent evaluators also supplied avenues for scrutiny. In practice, evidence raises substantial concerns. Direct cash programs were described as vulnerable to patronage, some selection rules and target populations were unclear, monitoring and payment irregularities affected social programs, and presidential rhetoric and budget practices blurred welfare with political loyalty. Migrants, Indigenous people, critics, feminists, journalists, and defenders experienced discriminatory or punitive treatment, while detention and deportation practices violated due process and non-refoulement protections. Some courts and autonomous institutions provided remedies, but enforcement and appeals were weak or incomplete. The evidence supports formal non-politicization commitments but mixed and often inadequate administrative protection against favoritism, punishment, or exclusion.","supporting_evidence_ids":["BATCH-0038-E005","BATCH-0051-E003","BATCH-0051-E004","BATCH-0049-E001","BATCH-0015-E004","BATCH-0015-E005","BATCH-0031-E019"],"contrary_or_qualifying_evidence_ids":["BATCH-0013-E009","BATCH-0016-E003","BATCH-0018-E006","BATCH-0031-E015","BATCH-0050-E002","BATCH-0026-E010","BATCH-0015-E003","BATCH-0021-R01-E014","BATCH-0049-E011"],"limitations_and_gaps":["Direct evidence of presidential ordering of welfare discrimination is limited.","Many findings concern program vulnerability or administrative practice rather than proven partisan allocation in every case.","Appeal outcomes and remedial compliance are incompletely documented."]},{"question_id":"6B.8","answer":"The period included meaningful formal rights advances: nationwide same-sex marriage, gender-marker changes, disability-rights reforms, older-persons protections, abortion-law expansion, labor reforms, migrant safeguards, and IMSS-BIENESTAR commitments to dignity, accessibility, informed consent, confidentiality, and non-discrimination. Mexico also maintained autonomous complaint, judicial, and human-rights institutions, and courts delivered some important remedies. Practical equality remained poor. Gender violence, femicide impunity, attacks on journalists and defenders, arbitrary detention, migrant and Indigenous discrimination, disability-access gaps, inaccessible information, inadequate shelters, and weak enforcement persisted. The CNDH found low compliance with recommendations concerning accessibility, Indigenous rights, disability services, discrimination, and protection systems; an academic study found femicide laws did not reduce violence. Thus legal conduct and institutional remedies were real, but implementation, incidence, and effective remedy were insufficient, and several protections were advanced by Congress, courts, autonomous bodies, or international partners rather than personally by the president.","supporting_evidence_ids":["BATCH-0003-E007","BATCH-0003-E013","BATCH-0013-E008","BATCH-0051-E003","BATCH-0041-E004","BATCH-0021-R01-E010","BATCH-0052-E010","BATCH-0015-E016"],"contrary_or_qualifying_evidence_ids":["BATCH-0006-E006","BATCH-0051-E009","BATCH-0048-E011","BATCH-0048-E013","BATCH-0046-E007","BATCH-0049-E011","BATCH-0008-E005","BATCH-0041-E004"],"limitations_and_gaps":["Legal changes are not evidence of uniform implementation or remedy.","The index lacks comprehensive 2023 incidence data for each protected group.","Attribution is often institutional or judicial rather than personal presidential authorship."]},{"question_id":"6B.9","answer":"The administration created or expanded durable-looking institutions and statutory frameworks: the Welfare Secretariat, universal pension, IMSS-BIENESTAR, child-protection routes, CONEVAL-linked planning, evaluation systems, disaster mechanisms, and formal health oversight and citizen-participation structures. IMSS-BIENESTAR rules supplied authority, facility networks, indicators, audits, professional training, complaint systems, and external evaluation; CONEVAL remained a functioning evaluation institution. Yet durability and resilience were undermined by repeated health-system transitions, uncertain annual budget dependence, weak program logic, staffing and infrastructure shortages, centralization, austerity, under-resourced protection mechanisms, and pressure on autonomous regulators and oversight bodies. Some institutions operated through international or subnational partnerships, making personal-ruler attribution and post-rule resilience uncertain. The evidence supports institution-building in selected social programs, especially pensions and evaluation, but not a consistently professional, transparent, financially reliable social-service architecture resilient beyond López Obrador’s personal and political model.","supporting_evidence_ids":["BATCH-0051-E001","BATCH-0051-E002","BATCH-0051-E004","BATCH-0051-E005","BATCH-0051-E006","BATCH-0031-E019","BATCH-0015-E004","BATCH-0015-E019","BATCH-0052-E017"],"contrary_or_qualifying_evidence_ids":["BATCH-0032-E003","BATCH-0032-E010","BATCH-0013-E009","BATCH-0026-E014","BATCH-0026-E006","BATCH-0018-E014","BATCH-0018-E019","BATCH-0052-E015","BATCH-0041-E003"],"limitations_and_gaps":["The index does not observe post-October 2024 institutional survival or funding reliability.","Formal statutory durability is better documented than actual resilience under stress.","Some institutional changes were shared with Congress, courts, states, donors, or autonomous agencies."]},{"question_id":"6B.10","answer":"Ordinary people ended the supplied period with mixed life-chance changes. Poverty fell from roughly 41.9% in 2018 to 36.3% in 2022, labor poverty and real labor income improved in 2023, minimum wages rose substantially, pensions expanded, food and housing deprivations declined, and transfers produced a measurable aggregate poverty reduction. These gains are plausibly attributable in meaningful part to federal transfers, pension expansion, wage policy, and labor-market conditions, though remittances, recovery, subnational action, and external demand also contributed. Against this, extreme poverty remained roughly unchanged or rose in absolute numbers; health-service deprivation more than doubled, public care and education outcomes worsened, food and service gaps persisted in poor and Indigenous regions, and children, disabled people, women, migrants, and rural communities remained disproportionately disadvantaged. Crisis response and rights protection also left serious avoidable harms. The period therefore shows genuine but uneven improvement in income and selected protections, offset by deterioration in health access, institutional quality, dignity, and durable equality; the evidence is strongest through 2022 and incomplete for final 2023 outcomes.","supporting_evidence_ids":["BATCH-0003-E002","BATCH-0015-E009","BATCH-0032-E002","BATCH-0032-E004","BATCH-0032-E006","BATCH-0032-E009","BATCH-0054-E002","BATCH-0049-E003","BATCH-0046-E009","BATCH-0052-E019"],"contrary_or_qualifying_evidence_ids":["BATCH-0032-E003","BATCH-0032-E005","BATCH-0032-E007","BATCH-0032-E010","BATCH-0032-E011","BATCH-0053-E007","BATCH-0053-E010","BATCH-0046-E007","BATCH-0015-E010","BATCH-0050-E010"],"limitations_and_gaps":["The principal multidimensional poverty, health, education, and group-incidence data end in 2022.","No complete counterfactual separates federal policy from pandemic recovery, remittances, wages, donors, subnational government, and external shocks.","Durability beyond the ruler’s period and final 2023 outcomes are not established."]}],"cross_lens_observations":["The strongest favorable evidence concerns explicit welfare prioritization, transfers and pensions, minimum-wage policy, poverty reduction, and formal evaluation and health-rights frameworks.","The strongest adverse evidence concerns health-access deterioration, weak implementation and targeting, persistent group disparities, politicization or patronage risk, crisis-distribution failures, and weak enforcement of rights.","Formal laws, budgets, indicators, and institutions are better documented than executed service quality, actual uptake, remedies, and ruler-specific causal effects.","Most outcome evidence is lagged through 2022; 2023 evidence is strongest for budgets, institutional rules, evaluations, labor outcomes, and the Otis response.","No score is assigned."]}
